prompt: Roughly when was the Bronze Age?

choices.text: From about 3300 BC to 1200 BC
From about 1200 BC to AD 500
choices.why: 1200 BC is when the Bronze Age ended and the Iron Age began, with the discovery of steel.

choices.text: The 1300s
choices.why: By the 1300s, several European rulers were banning alchemy. The Bronze Age was thousands of years earlier, from about 3300 BC to 1200 BC.

choices.text: The late nineteenth century
choices.why: That's when the modern field of coordination chemistry emerged. The Bronze Age ran from about 3300 BC to 1200 BC.

explanation: The period from about 3300 BC to 1200 BC is often called the Bronze Age, when our ancestors first started using metal. Around 1200 BC the Iron Age began.

prompt: How did Bronze Age people make bronze?

choices.text: By mixing various elements with copper to make a strong alloy
By digging it up: bronze is a pure element found in nature
choices.why: Bronze is an alloy, made by mixing various elements with copper, not an element.

choices.text: By hardening rock, wood, and bone
choices.why: Rock, wood, and bone are what metal replaced. Bronze was made by mixing various elements with copper.

choices.text: By turning lead into gold
choices.why: That was the alchemists' goal, thousands of years later, and they never succeeded. Bronze is copper mixed with other elements.

explanation: During the Bronze Age our ancestors learned to mix various elements with copper to make a strong alloy, called bronze. It let them craft sharper knives and stronger weapons out of metal instead of rock, wood, and bone.

prompt: What marked the start of the Iron Age, around 1200 BC?

choices.text: Finding an even harder metal and a much stronger alloy, steel
The discovery of bronze
choices.why: Bronze defined the earlier Bronze Age, from about 3300 BC. The Iron Age began with an even harder metal and a much stronger alloy, steel.

choices.text: The first Gold Rushes
choices.why: Gold Rushes are much more recent. The Iron Age began around 1200 BC with an even harder metal and the alloy steel.

choices.text: The alchemists' discovery of strong acids
choices.why: That came much later, from alchemy. The Iron Age began around 1200 BC with steel.

explanation: Around 1200 BC the human race found an even harder metal and discovered a much stronger alloy called steel. This period is known as the Iron Age.

prompt: Which list puts these in the right historical order, earliest first?

choices.text: Bronze Age, Iron Age, Werner's Nobel Prize, crystal field theory
Iron Age, Bronze Age, Werner's Nobel Prize, crystal field theory
choices.why: The Bronze Age (about 3300–1200 BC) came first. The Iron Age began around 1200 BC.

choices.text: Bronze Age, Iron Age, crystal field theory, Werner's Nobel Prize
choices.why: Werner won the Nobel Prize in 1913. Crystal field theory was developed soon after World War II.

choices.text: Bronze Age, Werner's Nobel Prize, Iron Age, crystal field theory
choices.why: The Iron Age began around 1200 BC, about three thousand years before Werner's Nobel Prize in 1913.

explanation: The Bronze Age ran from about 3300 to 1200 BC, when the Iron Age began. Alfred Werner won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1913, and crystal field theory was developed soon after World War II.

prompt: The section says the existence of chemistry as a field owes much to gold. Why?

choices.text: Gold was valuable and hard to get legally, so alchemists tried to make it, and their techniques helped lead to chemistry
Gold was the first element ever discovered
choices.why: The section's point isn't about discovery. It's that gold was valuable, which drove alchemists to try to make it.

choices.text: Gold is the most reactive metal, so it was easy to experiment with
choices.why: The section's reason is gold's value: few people could legally get it, so alchemists tried to make it.

choices.text: Chemists ran the state's gold mines
choices.why: The state owned the gold mines. That made gold hard to get, which is what drove the alchemists to try to make it.

explanation: Gold was a valuable commodity, and in ancient Egypt and the Roman Empire gold mines were the property of the state, so few people could legally get any. Alchemists tried to solve this by making gold, and techniques from the European stream of alchemy ultimately influenced the development of chemistry.

prompt: What were the alchemists trying to create?

choices.text: The Philosopher's Stone, to transmute lead into gold
Steel, a stronger alloy than bronze
choices.why: Steel was discovered around 1200 BC, at the start of the Iron Age. The alchemists were after the Philosopher's Stone.

choices.text: A catalyst for making ammonia
choices.why: That's the Haber–Bosch process of the twentieth century. The alchemists wanted the Philosopher's Stone, to turn lead into gold.

choices.text: Prussian blue pigment
choices.why: Prussian blue was used as a pigment, not the alchemists' goal. They wanted the Philosopher's Stone, to turn lead into gold.

explanation: The alchemists, a varied group of scholars and charlatans, aimed to create the Philosopher's Stone, which would cause the transmutation of lead into gold.

prompt: Did the alchemists succeed in changing lead into gold?

choices.text: No, but they made several contributions to modern chemistry
Yes, by distilling lead
choices.why: Alchemists developed distillation, but they never turned lead into gold.

choices.text: Yes, but they kept their method secret
choices.why: Alchemists did keep their processes secret, but they were never successful in changing lead into gold.

choices.text: No, and they contributed nothing to chemistry
choices.why: They failed at making gold, but they discovered strong acids and bases, developed glassware and methods such as distillation, and improved metallurgy.

explanation: Although alchemists were never successful in changing lead into gold, they made several contributions to modern-day chemistry: strong acids and bases, glassware, methods such as distillation, crystallization, and sublimation, and better metallurgy.

prompt: Which are the three major streams of alchemy, according to the section?

choices.text: Chinese, Indian, and European
Egyptian, Roman, and European
choices.why: Egypt and Rome come up because their gold mines belonged to the state. The three streams of alchemy are Chinese, Indian, and European.

choices.text: Chinese, Indian, and Egyptian
choices.why: The three major streams are Chinese, Indian, and European, and it was techniques from the European stream that influenced chemistry.

explanation: Three major streams of alchemy are known: Chinese, Indian, and European, all with some factors in common. Techniques developed in the European stream ultimately influenced the development of the science of chemistry.

prompt: Which of these was discovered by the alchemists?

choices.text: Sulfuric acid, H2SO4
Steel
choices.why: Steel was discovered around 1200 BC, at the start of the Iron Age, long before alchemy.

choices.text: Bronze
choices.why: Bronze, copper mixed with other elements, defined the Bronze Age, from about 3300 BC.

choices.text: Buckminsterfullerene, C60
choices.why: Fullerenes are modern carbon materials studied alongside nanomaterials, not an alchemists' discovery.

explanation: The alchemists discovered strong acids and bases, including nitric acid (HNO3), sulfuric acid (H2SO4), hydrochloric acid (HCl), and sodium hydroxide (NaOH).

prompt: The alchemists discovered strong acids and a strong base. Which of these is the base?

choices.text: Sodium hydroxide, NaOH
Hydrochloric acid, HCl
choices.why: HCl, as its name says, is an acid. The base the alchemists discovered was sodium hydroxide.

choices.text: Nitric acid, HNO3
choices.why: HNO3 is one of the strong acids the alchemists discovered. The base was sodium hydroxide.

choices.text: Sulfuric acid, H2SO4
choices.why: H2SO4 is one of the strong acids. The base on the section's list is sodium hydroxide.

explanation: The alchemists discovered nitric acid (HNO3), sulfuric acid (H2SO4), and hydrochloric acid (HCl), all acids, as well as the base sodium hydroxide (NaOH).

prompt: Which laboratory methods does the section credit the alchemists with developing?

choices.text: Distillation, crystallization, and sublimation
Spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography
choices.why: These aren't on the section's list. It credits alchemists with glassware and methods for distillation, crystallization, and sublimation.

choices.text: Catalysis with organometallic compounds
choices.why: Organometallic catalysts were discovered in the 1950s. The alchemists developed distillation, crystallization, and sublimation.

explanation: Glassware for running chemical reactions was developed by the alchemists, as were methods for distillation, crystallization, and sublimation.

prompt: Which of these is a contribution of alchemy to modern chemistry, according to the section?

choices.text: Improving metallurgy and the extraction of metals from ores
The industrial synthesis of fertilizer
choices.why: Fertilizer comes from the Haber–Bosch process, developed in the early twentieth century.

choices.text: Theories of bonding in coordination compounds
choices.why: Those came after World War II: crystal field theory and ligand field theory.

choices.text: A shared, public system of symbols for recording results
choices.why: The opposite: each alchemist had his own code and kept his processes secret.

explanation: Alchemy helped improve the study of metallurgy and the extraction of metals from ores. More systematic approaches to research also developed, which allowed the discovery of atoms and laid the groundwork for the periodic table.

prompt: Why are many of the alchemists' recipes vague and unclear today?

choices.text: Each alchemist recorded results in his own code and kept his processes secret
They wrote in one shared alchemical language that has been lost
choices.why: There was no shared language: different scholars developed their own sets of symbols.

choices.text: They didn't record their work at all
choices.why: They did record it, but each in his own code, with the processes kept secret so others couldn't profit.

explanation: Each alchemist had his own code for recording his data, and the processes were kept secret so others could not profit from them. Different scholars developed their own sets of symbols.

prompt: By the 1300s, what had several European rulers done about alchemy?

choices.text: Declared it illegal, with strict punishments for practicing it
Made it an official state science
choices.why: Rulers didn't support it: several declared alchemy illegal and set out strict punishments for practicing it.

choices.text: Required alchemists to publish their recipes
choices.why: Rulers declared alchemy illegal and set strict punishments. Alchemists kept their processes secret.

explanation: Many alchemists were not very honest, taking money from noblemen by claiming to be able to make gold from lead. By the 1300s, several European rulers had declared alchemy illegal and set out strict punishments for those practicing it.

prompt: What is probably the oldest known inorganic compound?

choices.text: Prussian blue, a deep blue pigment
Bronze
choices.why: Bronze is an alloy, copper mixed with other elements, not a single compound.

choices.text: Sulfuric acid
choices.why: Sulfuric acid was discovered by the alchemists. The section names the pigment Prussian blue as probably the oldest inorganic compound.

choices.text: Steel
choices.why: Steel is an alloy. The section names the pigment Prussian blue as probably the oldest inorganic compound.

explanation: Inorganic compounds have been known and used since antiquity; probably the oldest is the deep blue pigment Prussian blue, Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3.

prompt: Prussian blue has the formula Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3. How many iron atoms are in one formula unit?
explanation: There are 4 iron atoms outside the brackets, and each of the 3 bracketed [Fe(CN)6] units has 1 more: 4 + 3 × 1 = 7 iron atoms.

prompt: Inorganic compounds such as Prussian blue have been used since antiquity. When was their chemical nature understood?

choices.text: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, when coordination chemistry emerged
In antiquity, when they were first used
choices.why: They were used for a very long time without anyone knowing their chemical nature.

choices.text: During the Bronze Age
choices.why: The Bronze Age was about metals and alloys. The chemical nature of compounds like Prussian blue wasn't known until coordination chemistry emerged.

choices.text: Only after World War II, with crystal field theory
choices.why: Crystal field theory later explained their properties, but their chemical nature became known earlier, as coordination chemistry emerged in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century.

explanation: The chemical nature of inorganic compounds like Prussian blue was unknown until the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, when the modern field of coordination chemistry emerged.

prompt: Much of what we know about inorganic chemistry is based on the work of, and debates between, which two chemists?

choices.text: Alfred Werner and Sophus Mads Jørgensen
Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch
choices.why: Haber and Bosch are behind the industrial ammonia process. The famous debates were between Alfred Werner and Sophus Mads Jørgensen.

choices.text: Two rival alchemists of the European stream
choices.why: The debates came as coordination chemistry emerged, in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, between Werner and Jørgensen.

explanation: Much of what we know about inorganic chemistry is based largely on the work of and debates between Alfred Werner (1866–1919) and Sophus Mads Jørgensen (1837–1914).

prompt: Who came out ahead in the Werner–Jørgensen debates, and what recognition followed?

choices.text: Werner, who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1913
Jørgensen, who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1913
choices.why: Werner succeeded in the debates, and it was Werner who won the Nobel Prize in 1913.

choices.text: Neither: the debates were never settled
choices.why: Werner succeeded in the debates, and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1913.

explanation: Alfred Werner succeeded in the debates with Sophus Mads Jørgensen, and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1913.

prompt: What happened to inorganic chemistry after Werner succeeded in the debates?

choices.text: It declined in popularity until the mid-twentieth century, when World War II stimulated renewed interest
It grew rapidly and steadily through the early twentieth century
choices.why: The field declined in popularity after Werner's success, until World War II stimulated renewed interest.

choices.text: It merged with organic chemistry
choices.why: The section describes a decline in popularity, then a revival after World War II, not a merger.

explanation: After Werner succeeded in the debates, inorganic chemistry declined in popularity until the mid-twentieth century, when World War II stimulated renewed interest. Important discoveries and theories followed in the post-war era.

prompt: How does the section compare crystal field theory (CFT) and ligand field theory (LFT)?

choices.text: They complement each other: CFT is simpler, LFT more accurate
They complement each other: LFT is simpler, CFT more accurate
choices.why: This is reversed. CFT is the simpler theory, and LFT the more accurate one.

choices.text: LFT disproved CFT, which is no longer used
choices.why: The two are complementary, not rivals: CFT is simpler and LFT more accurate.

choices.text: They explain organic reactions, not coordination compounds
choices.why: Both explain the properties of inorganic coordination compounds.

explanation: CFT and LFT are two critical and complementary theories that explain the properties of inorganic coordination compounds, CFT being simpler, and LFT more accurate.

prompt: What do crystal field theory and ligand field theory explain?

choices.text: The spectroscopic, chemical, and structural properties of inorganic coordination compounds
How carbon nanotubes conduct electricity
choices.why: Nanotubes conduct through their extended conjugated π systems. CFT and LFT explain the properties of coordination compounds.

choices.text: Why the alchemists failed to make gold
choices.why: CFT and LFT are theories of bonding in coordination compounds, explaining their spectroscopic, chemical, and structural properties.

choices.text: How ammonia is made industrially
choices.why: That's the Haber–Bosch process. CFT and LFT explain the properties of inorganic coordination compounds.

explanation: Crystal field theory and ligand field theory provide explanations of the spectroscopic, chemical, and structural properties of inorganic coordination compounds.

prompt: What does the Haber–Bosch process make?

choices.text: Ammonia, directly from elemental nitrogen and hydrogen
Nitrogen and hydrogen, by breaking down ammonia
choices.why: This is reversed: the process makes ammonia from N2 and H2.

choices.text: Steel, from iron
choices.why: Steel dates from the Iron Age. The Haber–Bosch process synthesizes ammonia.

choices.text: Sulfuric acid
choices.why: Sulfuric acid was discovered by the alchemists. The Haber–Bosch process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.

explanation: The Haber–Bosch process provides for the synthesis of ammonia directly from elemental nitrogen, N2, and hydrogen, H2: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g).

prompt: What kind of catalyst does the industrial Haber–Bosch process use?

choices.text: An inorganic oxide catalyst
An organometallic catalyst
choices.why: The organometallic catalysts of the 1950s catalyzed organic reactions. The Haber–Bosch process is catalyzed by an inorganic oxide.

choices.text: The nitrogenase enzyme
choices.why: Nitrogenase carries out the same reaction in plant roots, at mild conditions. The industrial process uses an inorganic oxide catalyst.

explanation: The Haber–Bosch process is catalyzed by an inorganic oxide catalyst, and is one of the world's most important industrial reactions.

prompt: When was the Haber–Bosch process developed?

choices.text: In the early twentieth century
In the 1950s
choices.why: The section's sentence says the 1950s, but its note explains that's wrong: the process was developed between 1909 and 1913, in the early twentieth century.

choices.text: During the Iron Age
choices.why: The Iron Age began around 1200 BC. The Haber–Bosch process was developed in the early twentieth century.

choices.text: In the 1300s, by alchemists
choices.why: The alchemists discovered strong acids and bases, not ammonia synthesis. The Haber–Bosch process dates from the early twentieth century.

explanation: The Haber–Bosch process was developed in the early twentieth century (between 1909 and 1913), as the section says after the equation. The earlier sentence placing it in the 1950s is wrong, as the section's note explains.

prompt: In the Haber–Bosch reaction, N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), how many moles of ammonia can form from 6 mol of H2, with plenty of N2?
explanation: The equation shows 3 mol of H2 making 2 mol of NH3, so 6 mol H2 × (2 mol NH3 / 3 mol H2) = 4 mol NH3.

prompt: What has the Haber–Bosch process done for the world?

choices.text: Produced an enormous quantity of fertilizer, vastly increasing global food production
Made steel cheap enough for buildings and machines
choices.why: Steel comes from iron, not from this process. The Haber–Bosch process makes ammonia, the basis of fertilizer.

choices.text: Replaced gold, silver, and copper as currency
choices.why: The section notes those metals still serve as currency. The Haber–Bosch process gave the world fertilizer.

explanation: Since its development in the early twentieth century, the Haber–Bosch process has led to the production of an enormous quantity of fertilizer, vastly increasing global food production.

prompt: Which statement about the Haber–Bosch process and the human body is correct?

choices.text: A significant fraction of the nitrogen in a typical human body is estimated to come ultimately from the process
All of the nitrogen in the human body comes from the process
choices.why: That overstates it: the estimate is a significant fraction, not all of it.

choices.text: None of it: nitrogen from fertilizer never reaches people
choices.why: Fertilizer nitrogen ends up in our food. A significant fraction of the nitrogen in a typical human body is estimated to come from this process.

explanation: Because the Haber–Bosch process makes so much of the world's fertilizer, it is estimated that a significant fraction of the nitrogen content in the typical human body is ultimately derived from it.

prompt: How does the industrial Haber–Bosch process compare with the nitrogenase enzyme in plant roots?

choices.text: The industrial process needs high temperatures and pressures; nitrogenase does the same reaction at the mild conditions in soil
Nitrogenase needs high temperatures and pressures; the industrial process works at mild conditions
choices.why: This is reversed. The industrial process needs high temperatures and pressures, and the enzyme works at mild conditions.

choices.text: Both need high temperatures and pressures
choices.why: The enzyme carries out the reaction at the mild conditions within the soil. That contrast is what made it worth studying.

choices.text: Nitrogenase breaks ammonia down into nitrogen gas
choices.why: Nitrogenase carries out the same reaction as the industrial process, making ammonia from nitrogen.

explanation: The industrial reaction must be run at high temperatures and pressures, yet the nitrogenase enzyme in the roots of plants can carry out the same reaction at the mild conditions within the soil.

prompt: Why was the link between the Haber–Bosch process and the nitrogenase enzyme important?

choices.text: It drove research into enzymes' metal cofactors to improve inorganic catalysts, an early bridge between organometallic chemistry and biochemistry
It showed that enzymes contain no metals
choices.why: The research focused on the metal cofactors in enzymes, to learn how to improve inorganic catalysts.

choices.text: It ended research into industrial catalysts
choices.why: The opposite: it prompted intense investigations aimed at improving inorganic catalysts.

choices.text: It proved ammonia can only be made by living things
choices.why: The industrial process makes ammonia without living things, at high temperatures and pressures.

explanation: Intense investigations were aimed at improving inorganic catalysts by understanding the metal cofactors in enzymes. The link between the Haber–Bosch process and nitrogenase was an early bridge between organometallic chemistry and biochemistry.
